name: Sooyeon, community-college transfer
university: Transfer admission to UC Berkeley and UCLA
projectTitle: Why is choosing gummies so hard? A published team paper, then admission to UC Berkeley
description:
Sooyeon loves gummies. Choosing them is another matter: in a supermarket candy aisle she could stand for what felt like all day, weighing one bag against the next and unable to decide. In a research course in Seoul, that habit became a behavioral-economics paper on why shoppers agonize over small choices, and the team paper she worked on was published in a journal. In April 2026, she was admitted as a transfer student to both UC Berkeley and UCLA.

## An unlikely starting point

Sooyeon did not come from an international school. She graduated from a Korean high school, and when her university admissions in Korea did not go the way she had hoped, she enrolled at a community college in the United States to work toward a transfer. She came to CRI as a first-year student there.

Her English was far from fluent, and writing an academic paper in English was hard even to picture. The word "paper" alone sounded so imposing that she hesitated to begin.

## From sweeping topics to one small habit

Like many first-time researchers, Sooyeon assumed a paper had to announce a world-changing discovery or wrestle with a dense academic theory. She was eager to finish one, but the topics she brought in were so broad and ambitious that they would have challenged an undergraduate. Each time, she lost her footing.

The turning point came in a casual conversation about everyday life, when her professor heard about the candy aisle. Sooyeon weighed so many factors that she could barely settle on a bag. It was a serious case of indecision, the kind most people would laugh off as a harmless quirk.

CRI saw it differently and put a question to her: "Then why don't we find out, academically, why choosing gummies is so hard for you?" The focus broadened from gummies to snacks, among the most ordinary things people buy, and to the psychology of why shoppers deliberate irrationally before they decide. The paper that came out of it is titled **"Understanding the Interplay between Cognitive Biases and Heuristics in Consumer Behavior."** A frustration Sooyeon lived with every day had become the seed of a research project.

## Learning to think like a behavioral economist

To study the question properly, Sooyeon took a behavioral economics course in Seoul with Andrea Bernini, who teaches economics at the University of Oxford. Through that lens, her hesitation in the candy aisle touched two rich research areas: decision-making under uncertainty, and heuristics, the intuitive shortcuts people use to make judgments quickly.

She was skeptical at first.

> "Can choosing gummies really become a paper?"
> — Sooyeon, at the start of the project

Under Professor Bernini's structured guidance, she began to see how it could. He walked her through each stage, from sharpening an everyday puzzle into a precise research question to testing it against data. The study used statistical methods such as regression analysis, which high school students and early undergraduates rarely attempt, and that analytical work became Sooyeon's distinctive strength.

## A team split by strengths

English was still the biggest hurdle. For a student without an international-school background, writing an economics paper full of technical vocabulary felt close to impossible, and the CRI team still remembers how anxious she was.

> "My English is really weak. Won't I just be a burden to an Oxford professor and to teammates who are good at English?"
> — Sooyeon

CRI's answer is one it gives often: no one has to be good at everything alone. To play to her strengths, CRI placed her on a team with an international-school student who wrote fluent English and a US college student. Sooyeon and her international-school teammate divided the work cleanly:

- **Sooyeon** built the backbone of the research, handling the planning and the step-by-step logic of the data analysis.
- **Her international-school teammate** refined that work into polished academic English.

Each covered what the other lacked. The result was a paper Professor Bernini recognized as strong work, and the team went on to publish it in a journal. For Sooyeon, it was proof that imperfect English need not hold a student back when the teammates and the direction are right.

## Where the paper led

When she applied to transfer, the pieces fit together. A paper on cognitive bias in consumer behavior lined up directly with her intended major at UC Berkeley, Cognitive Science. To admissions readers, she would have stood out as more than a student with good grades: someone who could take a small, everyday frustration and investigate it with academic depth under an Oxford economist's guidance.

The decisions came that April: admission to both UC Berkeley and UCLA. When the news arrived, Sooyeon wrote to thank the CRI team, happier than anyone.

Her path holds a simple lesson for students who feel the way she once did. A small question, or even a personal weakness, can become serious research when it is developed with care, and shaky English or a paper that seems out of reach is a place to start rather than a reason to wait.

Students who want to turn an everyday question into research can start with the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp), where visiting professors from US and UK universities teach small groups in person in Seoul.

name: Anonymous student, stroke-risk model
university: Published paper on machine-learning stroke-risk prediction
projectTitle: Predicting stroke risk with machine learning: a high school student's published paper
description:
If you look at a person's age, blood glucose, body mass index and lifestyle together, can you tell in advance who is likely to have a stroke? One high school student built an entire research project around that question in CRI's 1-on-1 Advanced Research Program. The student designed the study from scratch, ran the analysis, and saw it through to a published academic paper.

Families often ask CRI two things: what does "doing research" actually involve for a high school student, and can a paper written by a teenager really count as a paper? This project may be the clearest answer to both.

## Catching risk before illness

The methods sound technical, but the core idea is simple. Analyze several health and lifestyle factors at once, and a model might pick out the people most likely to have a stroke before it happens. The project belongs to preventive medicine: rather than treating patients once they are ill, it aims to find the risk early enough for a stroke to be prevented.

## Putting several models to the test

To test the idea, the student compared several data-analysis methods. The most accurate was a random forest, a machine-learning technique that never decides on the basis of a single criterion. Instead, it weighs many decision rules at once and reaches a conclusion from all of them together.

On the paper's dataset, the random forest correctly identified about **98% of the people who actually had a stroke**. In other words, it rarely missed a true case. For a screening tool, missing as few real cases as possible is the priority, so this is a result with genuine medical relevance, not just the output of a computer analysis.

## Explaining the why

What lifts the paper above a report full of numbers is the explanation that follows them. The student worked through why the model behaved as it did and which variables mattered most. The paper explains, for example, why risk rises with age and why managing blood glucose and body weight matters, tying each point to existing medical research.

![Table titled Feature Importance Analysis ranking ten features, led by age at 0.348, average glucose level at 0.163 and BMI at 0.138](/editorial/224143561310-03.jpg "An excerpt from the student's published paper: the ten features that weighed most heavily in predicting stroke risk.")

In the paper's feature-importance ranking, age leads by a wide margin (0.348), followed by average glucose level (0.163) and BMI (0.138). Marital status, hypertension, residence type, gender, work type and smoking status round out the top ten, each with a much smaller weight.

The student then took one more step and set out how the analysis could be used in hospitals and wider healthcare systems. The finished paper runs the full course from research to interpretation to real-world application.

## Mentored by a USC data science professor

The project was supervised one-on-one by Cosimo Arnesano, a data science professor at USC. Alongside his university research, Professor Arnesano brings extensive industry experience: he was in charge of data-driven decision-making at global biotech and healthcare companies.

That background shaped how he mentored. Getting a model to run well mattered less to him than what the results actually meant, and he kept pressing the student on exactly that point.

## Justifying every choice

The student met Professor Arnesano regularly in one-on-one sessions. At every stage, from framing the research question and choosing methods to interpreting results and structuring the paper, the student explained their own reasoning and got feedback on it. The guidance was rarely "do it this way." Far more often it was "tell me why you thought that."

## What the student took away

The project left the student with more than a paper. It gave them confidence in three things: forming a question on their own, finding a way to answer it, and explaining the results logically.

That confidence becomes a powerful story in college essays and interviews. When someone asks "Why this major?", the student can answer with real research experience and real results instead of an abstract interest.

## Is 1-on-1 research right for you?

CRI does not recommend the 1-on-1 program to every student. It suits those who already have a reasonably clear field of interest or want to find one, and those who want an experience that leaves something concrete behind, such as a paper or other research output, as evidence of how they have grown. For those students it can be the most intensive choice open to them, and this project shows what it makes possible. Explore the [1-on-1 Advanced Research Program](/research/1-on-1) to see how an individual project comes together.

name: D., SRP 2025 Extension, carbon capture
university: Two published papers: co-authored at SRP 2025, single-author in the SRP Extension
projectTitle: From comparing carbon-capture solvents to redesigning the process: two published papers
description:
In Caltech chemist Brian Stoltz's class at the 2025 Seoul Research Program (SRP), D. and a classmate wrote a paper comparing three solvents that pull carbon dioxide out of smokestack gas, and it went on to be published in an academic journal. The newest of the three, a blend called CESAR-1, looked like the most promising, with one catch: under certain conditions, it can form byproducts that may cause cancer. In the SRP Extension, a follow-on program in which students dig deeper into the topic they began over the summer, D. went back to that catch and built a second paper around it, this time as the sole author. That paper was published too.

## Carbon capture, briefly

Carbon capture is a technology for picking carbon dioxide (CO₂) out of the exhaust, or flue gas, that leaves factory and power-plant smokestacks. Think of a filter that catches one ingredient in the smoke and lets the rest pass. The chemicals that grab the CO₂ are known as amine solvents.

## The first paper: which solvent works best?

The co-authored paper asked which amine solvent does the job most efficiently. The two students focused on three:

- **MEA**, the oldest and most widely used
- **MDEA**, studied as an alternative to MEA
- **CESAR-1**, a newer-generation blended solvent

They analyzed each one systematically: how well it captures CO₂, how much energy it takes to release the captured CO₂ again, and what side effects it brings, from damage to equipment to hazardous compounds.

The result was a review and comparison that showed, at a glance, how far carbon-capture technology has come. It made a clear case that CESAR-1 could be a more efficient alternative to the older solvents. It also flagged one important limitation: under certain conditions, CESAR-1 can generate harmful byproducts with carcinogenic potential.

## A sharper question

That limitation is where D.'s Extension project began. The first paper had asked which solvent is better. The single-author paper asks something harder: once CESAR-1 is running at a real industrial site, what is the biggest obstacle standing in its way?

D.'s answer pointed beyond CO₂ to the nitrogen oxides (NOₓ) that arrive mixed in with the flue gas. When these gases meet CESAR-1, the solvent becomes more likely to break down or to produce harmful compounds.

## Fixing the process, not the solvent

Here the paper changes approach. Rather than swapping CESAR-1 for yet another chemical, D. redesigned the process around it. The idea is to strip out the NOₓ with a selective catalytic reduction (SCR) unit before the flue gas ever reaches the carbon-capture equipment. SCR uses a catalyst to convert NOₓ into harmless nitrogen (N₂) and water (H₂O), and it is already a proven technology in many industries.

By placing SCR at the front of a CESAR-1 capture system, D. proposed an integrated process designed to sharply reduce both solvent breakdown and the formation of harmful byproducts. In the paper's flow diagram, ammonia is mixed into the flue gas ahead of an SCR reactor that uses a manganese- or cerium-based catalyst. The cleaned gas is then cooled and sent to the absorber, where CESAR-1, a blend of the amines AMP and piperazine, takes up the CO₂. A stripper releases that CO₂ into a storage container and returns the solvent to the absorber.

![Flow diagram in which flue gas passes through a heat exchanger, a heater and an SCR reactor fed with aqueous ammonia, then a cooler, an absorber containing CESAR-1 solvent, and a stripper that sends CO₂ to a storage container](/editorial/224143818942-04.jpg "Figure 8 from D.'s single-author paper: the proposed SCR-CESAR system, which removes NOₓ before CO₂ is captured")

## From summarizing to solving

Side by side, the difference is clear.

| | Co-authored paper (SRP 2025) | Single-author paper (SRP Extension) |
|---|---|---|
| Question | Which amine solvent captures CO₂ most efficiently? | What most limits CESAR-1 in industrial use, and how can that be reduced? |
| Approach | Compared MEA, MDEA and CESAR-1 on capture, the energy needed to release CO₂, and side effects | Redesigned the process by adding an SCR stage that removes NOₓ before capture |
| Contribution | Laid out CESAR-1's promise and its byproduct problem | Proposed a system-level design to cut solvent breakdown and harmful byproducts |
| Outcome | Published | Published |

The first paper organized what is already known. The second set out to solve a problem the first had exposed. That move, from organizing information to solving a problem, is what "going deeper" meant for D. in the Extension.

## What the Extension is for

D.'s case shows that the Extension is about more than writing one more paper. It means rereading finished group research, finding the question it left open, making that question your own, and carrying it through to a single-author paper and publication. Along the way, a student moves from someone who kept up well in class to someone who thinks like a researcher and designs research questions.

Both of D.'s papers trace back to one small-group summer course. To see how that course format works, and how students carry a summer paper forward afterward, start with the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp).

name: S., US boarding-school student
university: Admitted to Harvard in the early round
projectTitle: How a question about ketamine became a research paper and a Harvard admission
description:
How can one drug work as an anesthetic and also as an antidepressant? S., a student at a US boarding school, turned that puzzle about ketamine into a research paper in 2025 and was admitted to Harvard in the early round.

When CRI shares news like this, families almost always ask the same thing first: was this student exceptional from the start? What set S. apart was not a finished résumé. It was a single, consistent line that ran from interest to inquiry, from inquiry to a paper, and from the paper to an intended major.

## Curiosity that kept asking why

Brain science, mental health, and the ways drugs shape human behavior and cognition had held S.'s attention since high school. This went well beyond "I want to go to medical school" or "I want to study biology." It was curiosity that asked for reasons:

- Why don't antidepressants take effect right away?
- Why does the same drug act so differently from one person to the next?
- What actually happens in the brain to make emotions change?

The challenge was turning that curiosity into something a college could trust as real evidence of fit for a major. That bridge turned out to be a research paper written with CRI.

## One drug, two very different jobs

In 2025, S. joined a CRI research program and worked under Professor Jason Sello of UCSF (University of California, San Francisco), bringing those long-standing interests straight into the project and narrowing them to one question: **why does ketamine act as both an anesthetic and an antidepressant?** Put more broadly, how can a single drug play entirely different roles in the brain?

That was the moment a personal interest became a research question. The paper worked through the problem in stages:

- the limitations of conventional antidepressants
- why ketamine acts so quickly
- how blocking NMDA receptors changes the brain's neural circuits

The project then widened to ketamine's potential as a treatment for irritability associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). By analyzing the NMDA-receptor mechanism, the paper made a scholarly case for **drug repurposing**: taking a drug already in use and applying it to a different condition. In a later note, the student described the work as a paper "about the dual repurposing of ketamine." It was pharmacological analysis well past the usual high-school level.

## A complete line of reasoning

Every admissions reader is ultimately asking one question: can this student think like a scholar? The paper answered with a complete structure of thought. In it, the student:

1. posed the research question independently
2. analyzed the prior research
3. formed a hypothesis
4. explained the effect through its underlying mechanism
5. laid out the limitations

Nobody supplied a ready-made topic to follow. S. formed the hypotheses, argued them through with a faculty mentor, and produced a complete academic paper in English. That reasoning also held up outside the program: the paper cleared a journal's external review.

## The paper at the center of the application

S. submitted the paper with the college application, and it was never just one more line in the activities list. It became the starting point, and the evidence, for the questions every applicant has to answer:

- Why did I choose this major?
- How deeply have I already thought about this field?
- What do I want to explore further in college?

The application's argument, in effect, was this: I am not simply interested in this field; I have already explored it once, the way a researcher would. And Harvard admitted the student as an applicant planning to study exactly that field.

For an admissions officer, that is a very clear signal. The interest was proven through action, the action was documented in a paper, and the paper matched the intended major. In CRI's reading, Harvard most likely saw a student who had chosen a major on the strength of real research experience rather than on hope.

## A story anyone can check

Laid end to end, the path is easy to follow:

1. An interest that began in high school
2. That interest, shaped into a paper topic at CRI
3. The paper, taken through a journal's external review
4. The same topic, carried into the choice of major
5. Admission to Harvard

Each step explains the next, and each can be verified. That is why the result reads as a logical outcome rather than luck or clever packaging. After the decision, S. wrote to the professor who had guided the paper to share the news.

> "Thank you so much—I really couldn't have done it without you."
> — S., in a note to the faculty mentor

## Connecting an interest to a major

Many students tell CRI some version of the same thing: "I've decided on a major, but I don't know how to connect it to my applications." CRI's research programs are designed around that gap. Students turn an interest into a question, the question into a paper, and the paper into a story about their field. By the end, they can explain in one coherent account why they chose the major, what they have already done in it, and what they want to pursue next.

S. never dressed up a major to impress Harvard. The student took an interest that was already there and, at CRI, carried it through to a finished paper. That consistency and depth, backed by work anyone could verify, is what made the application stand out. If you have a question of your own, in pharmacology or any other field, explore CRI's faculty-guided [research programs](/research) to find the one that fits.

name: Jay, 1-on-1 program, rehab wearable
university: Poster at IEEE EMBS BSN 2025 (Body Sensor Networks)
projectTitle: Catching runner's knee before it hurts: a student's rehab wearable at IEEE BSN 2025
description:
Runner's knee has a way of coming back. Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) affects about 21 percent of recreational runners and often returns even after treatment, in large part because rehab exercises are easy to do wrong. Jay, a high school student in CRI's 1-on-1 Advanced Research Program, spent summer 2025 chasing a practical question:

> "Could I build a smart device that alerts me right before my movement turns unstable during rehab, or right before the pain starts?"
> — Jay, on the question behind the project

That question became a working wearable, a machine-learning model, and a research poster on a real-time rehabilitation system for runners with PFPS. Jay presented it at IEEE EMBS BSN 2025, the International Conference on Body Sensor Networks. Few high school students reach an international conference with research they carried out on their own, which made this a milestone for Jay and for CRI.

## A mentor who studies behavior through sensors

Jay's faculty mentor was Nabil Alshurafa, an associate professor at Northwestern University's Feinberg School of Medicine and McCormick School of Engineering. A leading expert in digital health, he uses wearable sensors and AI to analyze human behavior. He co-directs Northwestern's Center for Behavior and Health, serves as principal investigator on NIH R01 research, and has led many studies on AI-based behavior analysis, stress detection, and monitoring of eating habits.

His research starts from questions buried in smartwatch and sensor data. When do people feel stress? At what moment does a rehab movement start to falter? How can technology change health? Beneath them sits a larger one: can technology help us understand human behavior better, and nudge it in a healthier direction? A project on predicting knee pain during rehab fit squarely inside that agenda, and the overlap is a large part of why Jay's experimental design and analysis could be so careful.

In their meetings, Professor Alshurafa kept returning to the basics: "What does this data mean for a person?" and "What would we actually need to detect for this to help?" That focus is what turned a simple experiment into research worth the attention of working scientists. Jay's poster thanks him and the HABits Lab for their guidance and advice throughout the research design and process.

## A TA for the hardest parts

Jay also had a teaching assistant from UC Berkeley, a mentor with extensive research experience in biosignal processing (ECG, IMU, and GSR), Python data analysis, machine-learning preprocessing and modeling, and health-data visualization. The TA's job was not to do the work but to keep Jay moving, sharing practical tips so Jay could handle experiment design, code debugging, and model tuning independently. Together they worked through two of the most demanding steps: preprocessing the IMU instability data and optimizing the Random Forest model.

## Step 1: Listening to runners and experts

Jay began with the people who live with the problem. A survey went out to running communities in the United States and Korea, asking questions such as "What was hardest about rehab?" and "When does the pain come back?"

Jay then interviewed five experts in depth, whose experience ranged from sports rehabilitation for the International Olympic Committee and Korea's national team to hospital research. A clear theme emerged: people rehabbing on their own, without personalized guidance, can choose the wrong exercises or loads and make their symptoms worse. What they needed was a system that could catch the early signs of PFPS so they could correct course before the pain set in.

## Step 2: Building the wearable

Those findings shaped the device. Jay combined three sensors into a single rehab wearable:

- **IMU** (a 6-axis inertial measurement unit) to track movement
- **PPG** (photoplethysmography) to capture heart-rate signals
- **GSR** (galvanic skin response) to measure skin conductance, a marker of stress

A participant then performed lunges under four conditions, each designed to simulate a different physical state:

1. **Standard:** full range of motion at normal speed
2. **Slow:** the same exercise at reduced speed
3. **Small range:** limited knee bending
4. **Instability:** a deliberately wobbly movement, induced by attaching a 1 kg weight to the leg

The sensors recorded continuously throughout, and that data became the foundation for Jay's machine-learning model.

## Step 3: Teaching a model to spot trouble

Jay trained a Random Forest model on the sensor data, analyzing how each rehab movement changed the signals, from growing wobble to shifts in acceleration and GSR responses. The model learned to judge three things: whether a movement was stable, whether the rehab form was off, and whether the signals looked like the moments just before pain.

In practice, that meant teaching the classifier to tell the four lunge conditions apart, and it did so with **79 percent accuracy**. It was especially strong at picking out dynamic motions and unstable movement patterns, which are critical predictors of PFPS onset. The poster breaks the results down by condition: precision is how often the model was right when it named a condition, recall is the share of lunges of that condition it caught, and the F1 score balances the two.

| Lunge condition | Precision | Recall | F1 score |
|---|---|---|---|
| Instability | 0.90 | 0.90 | 0.90 |
| Slow | 0.57 | 0.67 | 0.62 |
| Small range | 1.00 | 0.80 | 0.89 |
| Standard | 0.71 | 0.71 | 0.71 |

On top of the classifier, a second layer watched for pain onset. It tracked the variance in the leg's acceleration in real time, and when the standard deviation climbed, it treated that as an early warning and lit an LED to alert the runner. Both layers ran on the device itself.

## Why it matters for runners

The project was built to help real people, and it points to three practical uses:

- **A warning before the pain.** When a movement starts to wobble during rehab, the runner gets immediate feedback through the LED alert.
- **Personalized rehab.** Because the system reads each person's own movement data, it could support faster, more precise rehab guidance.
- **Rehab at home.** The design could grow into a home rehabilitation tool, an area of active research at Northwestern's medical school.

Jay's poster sets out the next steps: testing with a larger sample, evaluating the system in real time, and adjusting a person's rehab program when the system detects pain.

## Poster day at BSN 2025

At the conference, Jay stood by the poster and explained the work to researchers from around the world. The questions kept coming:

- Why these particular sensors?
- How did you capture the signals that come just before pain?
- How did you detect instability?
- What would it take to raise the model's accuracy?

The researchers showed keen interest in Jay's approach and analytical skill.

Jay was not the only CRI student at BSN 2025. Four teams from Professor Alshurafa's wearable-health course in the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp) also presented posters at the conference, and their story is on the [Student Success](/success/srp-teams-wearable-health-ieee-bsn-2025) page.

## What made it work

Jay's project follows the structure of CRI's [1-on-1 Advanced Research Program](/research/1-on-1). Each student is matched with a professor from a leading university, learns the experimental protocols used in that professor's own lab, and drives the project from choosing the topic through the experiment and analysis. The goal is a real paper rather than coursework, and when the work is ready, that paper can go on to a conference presentation or journal submission, the way Jay's question about runner's knee ended up on a poster board at BSN 2025. The program runs year-round, and most projects take two to four months.

name: Y., hotel housekeeping economics paper
university: Admitted to NYU in Early Decision
projectTitle: Why hotels reward guests who skip housekeeping: a screening model and an NYU admission
description:
"I get that hotels cut back on housekeeping to help the environment. But why do some hotels give you points for skipping it?" That question about an ordinary hotel policy led Y. deep into economic theory. Working with Professor Ryan Fang of the University of Chicago in a CRI research program, he turned it into a full paper: "To Change Linen or Go Green: Hotel Housekeeping Service Offering as a Screening Problem." The finished paper, backed by a strong recommendation letter from Fang, went into Y.'s Early Decision application to New York University, and he was admitted.

## A mentor in the economics of information

Fang works in game theory and information economics, the mathematical study of how what people know, and what they don't, shapes the choices they make. His research asks how the flow of information drives the decisions of individuals, firms and governments, and what economic equilibrium results. These are advanced topics even at the graduate level, and Fang's teaching demands that kind of rigor. He is also known for showing students how to connect the theory to real social behavior.

## A problem of hidden information

Y. began with a problem economists call **asymmetric information**. A hotel cannot see what each guest actually wants. Some guests want fresh sheets every day; others care more about the environment or their privacy. Each guest's true "type" is hidden, which leaves the hotel with a practical puzzle: how do you offer the best service when you don't know what your customers prefer?

His hypothesis was that cutting back on cleaning might be more than a cost-saving move. It could be a strategic tool for telling guests apart, a practice economists call **screening**.

## Letting guests reveal themselves

In screening theory, a seller who can't observe a buyer's type designs a menu of options that leads buyers to sort themselves. Instead of offering every guest the same stay, the hotel in Y.'s model offers two:

- **Option A:** daily housekeeping at price *P*
- **Option B:** no housekeeping, plus a points reward *r*, for an effective price of *P* − *r*

The choice itself becomes the signal. Guests who prize cleanliness pick Option A. Guests who care more about the environment, or about saving money, pick Option B.

Y. then wrote the problem down mathematically, modeling the hotel's profit and the guest's utility. A guest's utility depends on whether the room is cleaned and on the price paid. The hotel pays a cost *C* every time it cleans, and its profit depends on which option each guest takes. To keep the problem tractable, he reduced it to two kinds of guest, a high-value type and a low-value type, who differ in how much they value housekeeping. The hotel can offer each type its own package, but the pair has to satisfy two conditions at once:

- a **self-selection constraint**, so that each type prefers the option designed for it, and
- a **participation constraint**, so that each type is still willing to book.

Together, these conditions keep guests honest: each picks the option that matches their real preferences instead of posing as the other type.

![Game tree diagram: a hotel node at the top leads to a nature node that splits guests into Type I and Type II, and each guest then chooses O1, O2 or Leave, with payoff pairs such as (P-C, V+l-P) and (P-r, V-P+r)](/editorial/224078682732-03.jpg "The game tree from Y.'s paper: the hotel sets its offer, each guest turns out to be Type I or Type II, and the guest chooses daily cleaning (O1), skipping it for a reward (O2) or leaving.")

## What the model showed

Solving the model gave Y. three results, each driven by how much housekeeping costs the hotel:

1. **When cleaning is cheap,** the hotel should keep daily housekeeping as the standard service, with any reward for skipping it set below the lowest value a guest places on a cleaning. Because most guests care about clean rooms, keeping the service is what maximizes profit.
2. **When cleaning is expensive,** the hotel should make housekeeping optional, with a reward set above the highest value any guest places on it, so that guests give it up on their own. Costs fall, and guests stay satisfied.
3. **At intermediate costs,** the most interesting case appears. When the hotel offers both options, guests with different preferences naturally choose different ones.

That third outcome is what economists call a **separating equilibrium**: each type reveals itself through its own choice. Housekeeping, in other words, is more than a line on the cost sheet. It is an information tool that lets a hotel learn what its guests value and maximize its profit accordingly. Y. also argued that hotel housekeeping and pricing had been largely unexplored territory for information economics.

## Where green messaging meets incentive design

The paper impresses for more than the precision of its model. In his conclusion, Y. placed the work where ESG (environmental, social and governance) management meets behavioral economics. Hotels speak publicly about protecting the environment, yet underneath sits a deliberately designed economic incentive that steers what guests choose. The paper puts its finger on the line between ethical consumption and market strategy. As Y. wrote:

> "When companies put an environmental message forward, their strategy is evolving into one that draws on customers' psychological satisfaction."
> — Y., in his paper

The observation ties together three central themes in business today: sustainability, consumer psychology and the design of information.

## Built like university research

The paper has the architecture of university-level theoretical work:

- **Theoretical model:** asymmetric information and contract theory applied to a real business setting
- **Analytical derivation:** optimization under constraints to find the equilibrium
- **Paper structure:** a conventional progression from introduction to model, analysis and conclusion

Fang's recommendation letter made the same point. He wrote that Y. had grasped graduate-level information economics and could apply it independently.

## Treated as a colleague

Fang treated Y. less as a student than as a research colleague. At their weekly meetings he reviewed Y.'s modeling drafts, checked the equations for logical consistency and worked through the interpretation of the results with him. One piece of advice reframed the project:

> "Don't see housekeeping simply as a question of cutting costs. Try interpreting it as a strategic signal under asymmetric information."
> — Professor Ryan Fang, University of Chicago

That shift carried Y. beyond an analysis of an environmental campaign. His model showed that a hotel's housekeeping decision is an economic strategy built on what the hotel does and doesn't know about its guests.

In his letter, Fang described Y.'s thinking as the strongest he had seen among the high school students he had mentored. Y., he wrote, had learned to define a problem on his own and explain it in the language of economics, an academic independence he considered rare even at the graduate level.

## From a finished paper to NYU

With the paper complete, Y. applied to New York University under Early Decision, with Fang's recommendation letter in his file. What stood out in his essay and portfolio was the pairing of two threads: environmental sustainability and a real command of information-economics reasoning. NYU admitted him in the early round.

The paper mattered, but so did the process behind it. Y. had posed his own academic question and worked it through to an answer, which is exactly the kind of research-minded thinking universities look for.

His project drew on what CRI builds into its research programs: regular meetings with a faculty mentor from a leading university, technical support and feedback from TAs, and guidance through structure, analysis and writing all the way to submission. If an everyday puzzle has you wondering about the economics behind it, you can compare faculty-guided options on the [research programs page](/research).

name: K., Jeju international-school student
university: Published in IJHSR; admitted to Stanford and Oxford
projectTitle: Can tears cloud judgment? A Jeju student's Oxford-mentored study, published in IJHSR
description:
"Can tears cloud a person's judgment?" For K., an international-school student on Jeju in a CRI research program, that question became a full psychology experiment. In winter 2024, working with Robin A. Murphy of the University of Oxford, K. designed the study, ran it online with 40 adults and wrote up the results as a research paper. The paper went through formal peer review and was published in the *International Journal of High School Research* (IJHSR). In the admissions cycle that followed, K. was admitted to both Stanford and Oxford.

## A mentor who studies how minds learn

Murphy teaches in the Department of Experimental Psychology at Oxford. He is also Fellow and Tutor for Admissions at Corpus Christi College. His research spans learning, memory, cognition and psychopathology, and centers on associative learning in humans and animals: how we learn about the world, remember it and respond to it. Put simply, he asks why two people can go through the same experience and come away feeling and acting differently. He is especially known for work on how cognitive biases relate to the way we learn.

Murphy is regarded as a pioneer of computational psychopathology, a field that uses mathematical and computer models of learning to explain anxiety, depression and fear as errors in learning. He directs the Computational Psychopathology Research Group, and its findings feed into the scientific basis for treatment, including cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). Beyond the university, his lab has collaborated with companies and organizations including Siemens, Barclays Bank and Publicasity, applying what it knows about learning and decision-making to business, communication and risk assessment.

He has published widely in international journals and has long experience supervising students. His approach to teaching is exacting but warm:

> "It doesn't matter whether a student finds the 'right answer.' What matters is being able to explain, on their own, why they reached it."
> — Robin A. Murphy, University of Oxford

Murphy gives students direct feedback on everything from the fine logic of an experimental design to data interpretation, the ethics of testing a hypothesis and the rigor that psychological reasoning demands. Working from his feedback each week, K. refined the research question, adjusted the variables in the design and brought the paper to completion.

## Turning a premise into an experiment

The study started from an intriguing premise. When people see a face with tears on it, do they perceive that person as more helpless and more in need of help?

To test it, K. combined two core ideas in psychology. A **contingency judgment** is an estimate of how closely an action and an outcome are linked; **perceived agency** is how much control an observer believes someone has over what happens to them. Forty adults aged 21 to 52 took part online. On screen, they watched a rapid series of study-and-exam scenarios: the left side showed whether a person had studied ("STUDY" or not), and the right side showed whether that person "PASSED" or "FAILED."

Two factors varied, giving a 2×2 within-subject design in which every participant saw all four combinations:

- **Contingency.** In the positive condition, studying genuinely went with passing. In the zero condition, studying made no difference to the result.
- **Face.** The person on screen appeared either with tears or without them.

![Diagram of three stacked trial screens: a woman's face with STUDY and a PASSED stamp, a face-only fixation screen, and a face with STUDY and a FAILED stamp, labeled with 600 ms timings](/editorial/224075921009-04.jpg "Figure 1 of K.'s paper: each stream ran 40 rapid trials, with the cue and outcome shown for 600 ms, then a 600 ms fixation.")

After each run, participants rated on a scale from −10 to +10 how strongly studying predicted passing for that person. The score served as a measure of how much agency, or helplessness, the observer attributed to the person on screen.

## What the data showed

The pattern was clear. Participants who saw tearful faces judged the link between studying and passing to be weaker. Even when the situation was identical, the sight of tears seemed to lead them to an unconscious conclusion: this person can't change the outcome on their own.

Most striking, the effect held even in the positive condition, where studying really did pay off. With tears on the screen, participants could no longer tell the positive and zero conditions apart. An emotional cue had clouded a logical judgment.

K. proposed two explanations:

1. **Emotional salience.** People attend to emotional information before neutral information, so the emotional pull of tears may take up the cognitive resources needed for learning and judgment.
2. **Carryover effects.** Feelings stirred by seeing tears and failure in close succession may have spilled over into the judgments that followed.

The conclusion: tears are more than an expression of feeling. They act as a powerful signal that someone needs help, one strong enough to change how observers read that person's actions. The paper links this to the role crying plays in drawing social support. More broadly, the finding offers a clue to how people pick up on, and respond to, one another's emotions.

## Built like a university study

The project followed the conventions of university research from the start:

- The paper uses the standard IMRaD structure (introduction, methods, results and discussion).
- The study was approved by Oxford's Central University Research Ethics Committee (CUREC).
- K. built and ran the experiment online in Gorilla Experiment Builder.
- The 2×2 within-subject factorial data were analyzed with ANOVA.

That is the level of precision typically expected of undergraduate research. IJHSR's reviewers responded especially well to the way the paper tested an abstract question—how emotion and cognition interact—with quantitative data.

## Peer review at IJHSR

Published since 2019 by Terra Science and Education, a US nonprofit, IJHSR is an international journal devoted entirely to high school research. By the standards of journals open to high school authors, it is known for fairly rigorous review. Manuscripts are peer-reviewed by university faculty and other experts, and authors must suggest their own reviewers, so students experience how academic publishing actually works instead of simply submitting a file. The journal accepts both original research and literature reviews. Articles are open access and indexed in EBSCO and Google Scholar, where libraries around the world can find them.

K.'s paper, "Investigating the Influence of Tears-relevant Visual Cues on Contingency Judgments and Perceived Agency," appeared in IJHSR Volume 7, Issue 7 (2025), pages 18–22. The full paper is [available open access](https://doi.org/10.36838/v7i7.18).

## What came next

Once the paper was complete, Murphy gave his assessment:

> "This was high-caliber research that clearly demonstrated that emotional cues can disrupt learning-based judgments."
> — Robin A. Murphy, University of Oxford

Impressed by K.'s experimental design and interpretation, he also wrote a recommendation letter himself, citing K.'s attitude toward research, logical thinking and statistical skill. It was the kind of endorsement that carries real weight in a college application. That admissions season ended with offers from Stanford and Oxford.

For CRI, the publication was only part of the story. Just as important was how K. got there: staying with the question to the end, running the experiment and analysis with care, and learning to think like a researcher alongside a leading psychologist.

If you have a question of your own you want to test, the [1-on-1 Advanced Research Program](/research/1-on-1) builds an individually arranged project around one student and a faculty mentor, typically over two to four months, and CRI supports each manuscript through journal submission.

name: J., SRP 2025 Extension startup
university: Basketball stats app launched in Korea; US incorporation and beta planned
projectTitle: From a paper on mismatched ad pairings to a basketball stats app for amateur leagues
description:
After finishing a research paper on advertising in the summer of 2025, J. found himself asking a new question: could the thinking he had learned doing research be applied to something he loved, like sports? The answer became a statistics app for amateur basketball leagues, launched first in Korea, and an investor pitch deck built on US market data.

Most students treat a finished paper as the end of the road. In the SRP Extension, CRI's follow-on to the Seoul Research Program, it can be the starting point. There, the startup track led by MIT Sloan's Kit Hickey runs as a ten-week, one-on-one online internship, designed not as another line on a college application but as research-and-execution experience that can carry on into university. J. worked through it with Hickey and startup mentor VA7, turning an idea that grew out of his research into a business plan.

## A summer paper on mismatched pairings

J. started in the 2025 Seoul Research Program, where he completed a paper with Professor Kit Hickey of MIT titled **"The Power of Mismatch: How Incongruous Pairings Drive Ad Effectiveness."** As the title suggests, the paper looked at how pairings that seem not to fit can make an ad more effective, and it gave him practice in two things he would use again: structured, logical reasoning and data analysis.

It was those skills, more than the advertising topic, that J. carried forward. Applied to sports, a field he loves, they became the basis for his app. After releasing it in Korea, he continued in the Extension with a new goal: taking the product to the US market and setting up a company there.

## Two mentors, two roles

The startup track pairs a faculty member with a working entrepreneur, so a student gets both the academic framing and the practical execution. CRI calls this a "research-to-market" model.

### Professor Kit Hickey, MIT Sloan

Kit Hickey teaches entrepreneurship at the MIT Sloan School of Management. She is a serial entrepreneur and a former founding member of Draper Athena, and she leads the Extension's Business Plan Studio. Her focus is less on startup theory than on helping students take what they learned in research and translate the problem into the language of the market.

![Kit Hickey stands at the front of a classroom as two students present in front of a projected slide](/editorial/224074766455-04.jpg "Kit Hickey listens to a student presentation during SRP 2025 in Seoul.")

With J., she led three core sessions:

1. Structuring the problem and defining the market
2. The revenue model and a value-proposition framework
3. Coaching on the pitch-deck presentation

> "An idea starts with defining the problem. It becomes a business only when you can clearly say who your market and your customers are."
> — Kit Hickey, MIT Sloan School of Management

### Mentor VA7, CEO of Metana AI

VA7 holds a Master of Public Policy from the University of Chicago and co-founded Metana AI, an AI startup he now leads. The company uses AI to automate content production for global brands, Hilton among them. He won first place at the 2024 ETHDenver hackathon and has been selected for HashKey Incubator and AWS Activate.

On the track, VA7 handles the hands-on work. With J., he built out the market analysis, the structure of the pitch deck, and a roadmap for incorporating the company.

> "A pitch deck isn't about design. It's the structure of your thinking. You have to develop an eye for understanding the market."
> — VA7, CEO of Metana AI

## Inside the Advanced Business Plan Studio

The studio is a one-on-one program in which a student uses the thinking and data from summer research to produce an investor-grade business plan. It runs for 10 weeks and 18 hours in total: 3 hours with the professor and 15 with the mentor. J. planned to take it all the way to incorporating a real company.

| Weeks | Focus | What the student works on |
|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | Problem definition and customer research | Understanding the market's structure; competitor analysis |
| 3–4 | Value proposition and MVP design | User personas and feature design |
| 5–6 | Revenue model and pricing strategy | Comparing B2B and B2C models; customer acquisition cost (CAC) and lifetime value (LTV) analysis |
| 7–8 | AI-assisted pitch deck development | Visualizing material with ChatGPT and Gemini |
| 9–10 | US incorporation roadmap | Delaware corporate structure; building early partnerships |

## J.'s ten weeks, step by step

**Step 1: Define the problem.** With Professor Hickey, J. looked at a practical gap: amateur basketball leagues have very little data to work with. He settled on his core problem, which was that keeping stats is a hassle in high school and adult recreational leagues. He then used empathy maps and problem-tree analysis to divide his potential users into distinct groups.

**Step 2: Design the MVP and the business model.** Working with VA7, J. compared a B2B model, selling to schools and clubs, with a B2C model aimed at individual users, and studied the competition. Along the way he came up with the idea of adding AI camera technology. He also generated market reports automatically and used them to assemble a first draft of his pitch deck.

**Step 3: Finish the deck and prepare for the US.** J. tightened the deck's logic and revenue model, then rebuilt it as an investor-style presentation grounded in US market data. In the process he learned how a Delaware C-Corp is formed and how its funding can be structured.

**Step 4: Move toward incorporation and commercialization.** As of November 2025, J. and VA7 were working through the incorporation documents, the equity structure, and early funding simulations. He was also collaborating with a Korean company that has AI vision-recognition technology to improve the MVP, with a US beta launch targeted for the first half of 2026.

## From analysis to execution

CRI sees J.'s ten weeks as more than a startup exercise. He took the analytical habits he built while writing a paper and applied them to real business design and to a plan for expanding abroad. J. put it this way:

> "The paper was where my thinking began, and the internship was the process of applying that thinking to the world."
> — J., SRP 2025 and SRP Extension student

CRI's view is that colleges look at the process more than the result, and that the more hands-on the process, the more clearly a student's growth shows. In an application, a path like J.'s shows two things at once: intellectual depth and the ability to solve practical problems.

## Where a path like this starts

J.'s path began in a summer class in Seoul and continued with individual mentoring online. Students who want to take a finished paper further in a longer, individually mentored project can start by exploring the [1-on-1 Advanced Research Program](/research/1-on-1).

name: SRP 2024 team, Prof. Kavanagh's class
university: Systematic review published in a journal, with students as co-authors
projectTitle: From a first-day question to a published review of Korea's testing culture
description:
"What does learning usually feel like for you at school?" Professor Sarah Kavanagh of the University of Pennsylvania opened her class with that question on day one of the Seoul Research Program in summer 2024. Each high school student in the room had a different answer. One said they were used to being judged by test scores alone. Another said studying seemed to be about memorizing more than understanding. A third said teachers and students were both so busy that they sometimes forgot why they were learning at all.

That conversation turned into a research question: how does Korea's test-centered culture shape the way students experience learning? It is a topic everyone knows, yet one that has rarely been explored scientifically in any depth. By the end of the project, the team had written a systematic literature review on it, and the paper was published in a journal with the students as co-authors.

![A large group of students and faculty pose behind a banner reading "2024 Seoul Research Program: Exploring Innovative Education in Seoul"](/editorial/224073382390-04.jpg "Students and faculty of the inaugural Seoul Research Program, summer 2024")

## The professor behind the class

Sarah Schneider Kavanagh is an associate professor at Penn's Graduate School of Education (GSE) and director of the Collaboratory for Teaching and Teacher Education. She began her career teaching in secondary schools in California and Baltimore. Having seen the limits of teacher preparation firsthand, she has built her research around practice-based teacher education, looking past what teachers do in class to the reasoning and instructional strategies behind it.

She co-authored *Core Practices for Project-Based Learning: A Guide for Teachers and Leaders* (Harvard Education Press), which many US teacher training programs use as a text. Her work on teacher coaching, instructional practice and mentoring has been funded by Lucas Education Research, the Spencer Foundation and the McDonnell Foundation, and it reaches classrooms through partnerships with school districts, teacher training institutions and education nonprofits. She also leads TEDD (Teacher Education by Design), a teacher-learning platform used by school districts and teacher education programs in the US and abroad.

Her research spans the psychology of learning, pedagogy, social-emotional learning (SEL) and educational equity. Her classes start from questions students already live with: why the same lesson lands differently for different students, how a teacher's feedback shapes motivation and autonomy, and why socioeconomic background creates unequal chances to learn. Students test theories such as behaviorism, cognitivism and constructivism against problems like online learning, emotion regulation, motivation and achievement gaps. Every session, she gives specific feedback on their reasoning, writing structure and data interpretation, often pushing their thinking a step further with a simple question: "What theory could explain this sentence?"

![A professor holding a microphone speaks to students seated at dining tables in a room with tall windows](/editorial/224073382390-03.jpg "Professor Sarah Kavanagh talks with students over a meal")

## From complaints to a research question

Kavanagh's first lesson was how to find a problem worth studying.

> "Good research starts with curiosity. It isn't enough to criticize what you see. You have to be able to explain, with theory, why it happens."
> — Sarah Kavanagh, University of Pennsylvania GSE

The students began by listing problems they had noticed in their own school lives. One word kept coming up: *test*. One student described preparing for mock exams since middle school. Another talked about the anxiety of being caught between school grades and the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT). Every story led back to one question: "When did we stop learning and start studying for scores?"

## Seeing the problem through an ecological lens

Kavanagh then introduced Urie Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory.

> "Students don't learn alone. Home, the classroom, society and culture are all connected, and together they shape how a student learns."
> — Sarah Kavanagh

With that framework, the team set out to analyze how testing culture operates at three levels:

- **Individual:** motivation to learn, self-efficacy and stress
- **Microsystem (relationships):** interactions between teachers and students, and the atmosphere among peers
- **Exosystem (society):** college admissions policy, parents' expectations and sociocultural values

## 498 studies, 46 kept

Then the research training began in earnest. Working in international academic databases, the students screened 498 Korean and international studies, set aside duplicates and less reliable work, and kept 46 for a systematic review.

At first the papers were hard going. "What's a p-value?" the students asked. "What does it mean that this is statistically significant?" But session by session, they began developing their own codes and sorting the literature into themes. Kavanagh gave them one piece of advice:

> "Don't try to understand every paper completely. Instead, work out how the researchers are looking at the problem."
> — Sarah Kavanagh

From then on, the students' summaries started to read like research, with sentences like these:

- "The finding that testing weakens students' motivation to learn appears consistently."
- "However, most studies overlook the sociocultural context."
- "Testing culture is not an individual student's problem but a structural product of the education system."

The review ultimately showed that most existing studies focus on individual psychology and shed too little light on the structural problems of the education system itself.

## What the paper argues

The team settled on a final title: **"A Systematic Literature Review of Korea's Testing Culture: Surveying the Landscape from an Ecological Perspective."**

The introduction sets out the competitive structure of Korean education, and the body uses the ecological framework to trace how testing affects students at each level. In the discussion, the students take a social perspective on why the testing culture has been so hard to change. Tests, they argue, are more than a way to assess students: they are a mechanism, embedded in sociocultural power structures, that constrains learning. The paper proposes directions for structural reform and ends on a clear message: educational success depends not on scores but on the quality of the learning experience.

The review was published in a journal. For the students, it was a milestone: the first time their names had appeared as co-authors on a published paper.

## From learners to researchers

The project changed how the students saw school. After finishing the paper, they said, they caught themselves wondering, whenever they watched a class, why it was assessed that way. Somewhere along the way they had stopped being only learners and started thinking like researchers. Kavanagh made the same point in her final feedback to the team:

> "Your paper isn't only about Korean education. It is a philosophical attempt to ask what learning is. You have already taken your first step as education scholars."
> — Sarah Kavanagh

The team started from a subject as familiar as testing and went beyond it to show for themselves that learning takes shape within relationships.

## Start with your own question

Education and psychology are fields where a student's own experience of school can become the research question. If something about the way you learn keeps nagging at you, [CRI's research programs](/research) pair students with university faculty who guide them from a first question to a finished manuscript.

name: S., SRP 2024 climate-finance paper
university: Co-authored a Penn Kleinman Center blog post; admitted to Stanford
projectTitle: From a climate-finance paper to a co-authored Penn blog post and a Stanford admission
description:
How can the world reach net zero faster? S.'s answer was built on rewards, meaning incentives for moving faster, and it appeared on the blog of a University of Pennsylvania policy center in a post co-written with Penn law professor William Burke-White. The work began in Seoul in the summer of 2024, when S. wrote a paper on closing the climate finance gap in Burke-White's class. The same research later became the backbone of S.'s application to Stanford University, where S. was admitted.

## A law professor's class in Seoul

S. took part in the 2024 Seoul Research Program, CRI's summer program in which visiting faculty from US and UK universities teach small groups in person. S.'s professor was William Burke-White of the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, founder and inaugural director of Penn's Perry World House and a former member of the State Department's Policy Planning Staff. His work spans international law, global governance, and climate change law. In class, he asks students to learn how to build an argument rather than memorize information, and he follows each student's reasoning and writing closely.

## A paper on the climate finance gap

S.'s project grew out of a conviction that young people can contribute to the global debate on climate policy. The subject S. settled on was climate finance and the way international net-zero policy is structured. The result was a paper titled **"Leveraging Public Finance to De-Risk Private Investments: Legal Mechanisms to Close the Climate Finance Gap."**

The title names both the problem and the proposed response. The problem is the gap between the money climate action requires and the money actually available for it. The response is legal: mechanisms through which public finance takes on part of the risk that keeps private investors away.

## Staying on as a research assistant

The paper was not the end of S.'s work with Burke-White. After the program, S. was selected as one of CRI's Research Assistants (RAs), a role that kept the exchange with the professor going.

In that role, S. took on the question of how to speed the move to carbon neutrality and built an answer around rewards, or incentives, for getting there sooner. That answer became a climate-policy post S. co-authored with Burke-White for the official blog of Penn's Kleinman Center for Energy Policy, putting S.'s name beside the professor's on a Penn website.

## The research at the center of a Stanford application

When S. applied to Stanford, this experience became the most important research-based storyline in both the written application and the admissions interview. It tied together three pieces of work: a paper completed under a Penn law professor, a research assistant role that continued after the program, and a co-authored post published by a Penn policy center. In the interview, S. explained the research topic by drawing on in-depth conversations with the professor, and those conversations proved a strong point in S.'s favor.

Burke-White also added his own voice. At the end of the course, he writes a Final Evaluation assessing each student's approach to research and quality of reasoning, and he bases the letters he writes for his strongest students on it. For S., he personally wrote a detailed, strongly supportive letter of recommendation based on the paper, and S. was admitted to Stanford.

## A relationship that outlasts the course

What sets Burke-White's class apart, in CRI's experience, is that the academic relationship with the professor continues after the final session. For S., a summer paper grew into ongoing research, a co-authored blog post, and a recommendation from a professor who knew the work firsthand. The lasting result was not a grade but a record of S.'s growth as a researcher.

Students drawn to international law, climate policy, or global governance can explore the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp), where visiting professors guide small groups from a first research question to a finished paper.

name: P., UC Berkeley Haas transfer (2025)
university: Transfer admit, UC Berkeley Haas Undergraduate Business Program (fall 2025)
projectTitle: From a consumer-bias survey experiment to a transfer admission at UC Berkeley Haas
description:
P. had a 3.77 GPA and an ambitious goal: transferring from a community college into UC Berkeley's Haas School of Business. On grades alone, that was a hard case to make. So he set out to show Haas something a transcript cannot, and he built it from a question about why shoppers so often make irrational choices. The result was an offer of admission to Haas's Undergraduate Business Program (Spieker) as a transfer student for fall 2025.

## Looking beyond the transcript

When P. first came to CRI for advice, he was studying at a community college and preparing his transfer applications. A 3.77 is a respectable GPA, but the transfer students Haas admits typically have grades near the top of the scale, and his numbers alone were unlikely to compete.

He began looking for another way to make a convincing academic case for himself, and he settled on research. The interest was already there. Growing up, he had watched his parents run their business and wondered what drove their customers' choices.

## A question about irrational buying

P.'s project asked how cognitive biases and heuristics, the mental shortcuts people use to decide quickly, shape consumer behavior. He carried it out in a CRI research program with faculty mentor Andrea Bernini, a behavioral economist at the University of Oxford whose work also covers research methods and who has consulted for the World Bank.

The topic sat squarely within behavioral economics and marketing science, two areas Haas emphasizes, so the link between his research and his intended major, Business Administration, was easy to see.

The work became a team paper: P. and two co-authors published **"Understanding the Interplay between Cognitive Biases and Heuristics in Consumer Behavior"** in January 2025. One of those co-authors, a fellow community-college student, tells her side of the same project on our [Student Success](/success/community-college-to-uc-berkeley-transfer) page.

## Designing the experiment

The project went well beyond summarizing the literature. The team ran the full cycle of empirical research, from experimental design to data collection and statistical analysis, and P. was involved at every stage:

- **Participants:** high school students at international schools and university students in Korea and China
- **Variables:** the anchoring effect, confirmation bias, the scarcity heuristic, and loss aversion
- **Analysis:** correlations between behavioral patterns in survey data gathered through an online poll

CRI's advisers judged the design to be on par with, or beyond, a typical undergraduate research methods course. For an admissions reader, it was concrete evidence that P. could handle junior-year coursework.

When P. later presented the study to younger CRI students, his slides laid out what the data showed. A single heuristic, such as scarcity, raised purchases only slightly. Combinations, such as scarcity paired with loss aversion, produced stronger irrational behavior, and under scarcity pressure participants often ignored the logic of cost. Anchoring together with confirmation bias actually reduced purchases, though the reasoning behind those choices stayed simple. The distortions were strongest when emotional triggers such as fear of missing out or regret came into play.

![P. stands beside a large screen showing a slide titled "Key Findings from the Research (02)" while students seated at tables listen](/editorial/224067659651-03.jpg "P. walks younger CRI students through the study's key findings.")

## How the application came together

CRI's advisers describe three qualities the Haas transfer review looks for beyond grades:

1. **Academic rigor and preparation:** foundational coursework in the major and a deeper understanding of it
2. **Intellectual curiosity:** a real sense of the problems in the field and the habit of investigating them
3. **Contribution to community and perspective:** the ability to turn an academic viewpoint into action

P.'s paper spoke to all three, and the rest of the application was built around it. His personal insight questions (PIQs), the University of California's application essays, presented the research not as one more activity but as an arc:

- **Motivation:** a curiosity about consumer psychology that began as he watched his parents' business
- **Execution:** designing the experiment and collecting and analyzing the data firsthand
- **Reflection:** what the results taught him about human irrationality, and about his own patterns of decision-making

The recommendation came from the professor who supervised the research, and it made the same case from another angle. It described P. as taking the initiative at every stage, from experimental design to interpreting the results, and as showing the independent thinking of an undergraduate researcher. The essays and the letter told one consistent story, built on the same piece of research.

| Area | Typical transfer preparation | What P.'s research added |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GPA | Compete on a very high GPA | A 3.77, backed by evidence of advanced ability in the major |
| Major fit | Business internships and activities | A behavioral-economics research topic tied directly to business |
| Academic rigor | Mostly general-education and introductory courses | An experiment he helped design and analyze, showing junior-year-level ability |
| Essays | A list of activities | A clear line from why this major, to how he investigated it, to what he learned |
| Recommendation | A general assessment based on class grades | A supervisor's specific account of his research and his thinking |

P. was one of the students Berkeley admitted from a pool of more than 23,000 transfer applicants, and CRI's advisers believe the paper is what set him apart. As they see it, a Haas transfer review comes down to one question: can this student contribute academically from the first semester? P.'s application answered with evidence a 3.77 could not supply on its own. He had already done research at the level of the major.

## Why research counts for more in transfer admission

P.'s case reflects a broader difference between first-year and transfer admission. First-year review estimates a student's potential; transfer review looks for proof that the student can already succeed in the major.

- **The college transcript comes first.** For junior transfers especially, college GPA and the rigor of major prerequisites outweigh the high school record. An economics applicant, for example, should complete microeconomics, macroeconomics, statistics, math, and econometrics, ideally at honors or advanced level.
- **Activities should go deep into the major.** Working as a professor's research assistant, writing an undergraduate research paper, or joining major-related conferences and projects says more than a long list of clubs or volunteer hours.
- **Essays answer two questions.** Why transfer now, and why study this major at this university?
- **Letters should come from college professors.** A professor who taught you in a major course or supervised your research can speak directly to whether you are ready for upper-division work.

A research paper ties these together. It demonstrates fit with the major and college-level ability, and it gives both the essay and the recommendation something specific to build on.

## Passing it on

P. later returned to CRI to share what he had learned with younger students, from how to write a paper to how to approach a transfer application. One of his slides, "Verdict (Lessons & Advice)," paired some real talk (not everything will go as planned) with four reminders: tell your story, give it your everything, stay grounded, and detach from the outcome.

Students drawn to questions like P.'s can explore [CRI's research programs](/research), where university faculty, including behavioral economist Andrea Bernini, have guided students from a first research question to a complete paper.

name: Four teams, SRP 2025 (Alshurafa class)
university: Four abstracts accepted as posters at IEEE EMBS BSN 2025, Los Angeles
projectTitle: Four student teams from Nabil Alshurafa's SRP 2025 class take sensor research to IEEE BSN
description:
Does exercise actually relieve academic stress, or does it only feel that way? Three students who met for the first time at CRI's Seoul Research Program in summer 2025, each a different age and from a different place, decided to measure it. They built their own wearable sensors with Arduino, had participants work through SAT problems while wearing them, and compared what happened after ten minutes of running, meditating, or scrolling on a phone.

Their abstract was accepted at IEEE EMBS BSN 2025, the International Conference on Body Sensor Networks, held in Los Angeles on November 3–5, 2025. They were not the only ones. Four teams from Northwestern University professor Nabil Alshurafa's class that summer had abstracts accepted for poster presentation, which put high school researchers in front of graduate students and established scientists in wearable health.

## A professor who studies behavior through sensors

Nabil Alshurafa is an associate professor at Northwestern's Feinberg School of Medicine and McCormick School of Engineering, where he co-directs the Center for Behavior and Health. A specialist in both preventive medicine and computer engineering, he works in behavioral sensing: using AI and sensor data to understand how people behave and to predict their health. His HABits Lab (Health Aware Bits Lab) uses AI to analyze eating, stress, sleep, and physical activity and to develop practical ways of managing health. His papers have won best-paper awards from ACM IMWUT and IEEE PerCom, and his research is funded by the National Institutes of Health, the National Science Foundation, and Google.

He designed his CRI course, **Behavioral Medicine and Bioengineering in Mobile Health: Advancing Health Sensors and Technologies**, around the sensors, data, and analysis methods his own lab uses. In effect, students spend ten days in a scaled-down version of a working lab, learning to study human health and behavior with wearable sensors.

![Professor Nabil Alshurafa stands in the center of a group of about a dozen students in front of floor-to-ceiling windows at night](/editorial/224064517758-02.jpg "Professor Alshurafa with Seoul Research Program students, summer 2025.")

Two teaching assistants worked alongside him:

- **Ryugwang (Josh) Jang**, a UC Berkeley student with research experience in biosignal processing and health data analysis, helped teams design experiments, debug code, and visualize results, pitching the analysis at a level high school students could own.
- **Wooyoung Kang**, a computer science graduate student at NYU at the time of the program, with an undergraduate degree from HKUST, co-founded a startup that uses AI to detect strokes and took first place among some 1,500 competitors at Hong Kong Techathon+ 2024. He coached students through data analysis and AI modeling.

Both TAs ran the work the way projects run in the professor's lab, so students were doing research, not just learning about it.

![A young man leans in beside a student to look at her laptop screen, with bagged electronic parts on the desk](/editorial/224064517758-09.jpg "Working through the data together at a laptop.")

## Ten days, from sensor to poster

| Days | Stage | What students did |
|---|---|---|
| 1–3 | Foundations | Learned how heart rate, galvanic skin response (GSR), blood glucose, and stress sensors work, and practiced reading what body data reveals about emotion and health |
| 4–6 | Question and design | Chose a research topic with Professor Alshurafa, then designed the experiment and the data collection themselves |
| 7–9 | Analysis and writing | Cleaned, analyzed, and visualized data in Python with TA support, then wrote the paper in Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion form |
| 10 | Presentation | Presented the finished paper to the professor in the format of a poster session at an international conference |

The questions came from the students. Would caffeine sharpen their focus? Could exercise take the edge off test stress? Teams turned questions like these into experiments they could run within days.

![A student leans over a desk, fitting components onto a small circuit board, with wires and a laptop nearby](/editorial/224064517758-10.jpg "Assembling sensor hardware during the course.")

## Breaking the cycle of stress

The stress team started with little more than a broad interest in academic stress. Round after round of discussion with Professor Alshurafa narrowed it to a question they could test: does exercise really help relieve it?

Their study, "Breaking the Cycle of Stress: Exercise as a Regulator of Academic Pressure," followed 12 participants aged 15 to 19. They were split into three groups (running, meditation, and a control group that scrolled on their phones), each with equal numbers of athletes and non-athletes. Participants wore the sensors through two 20-minute exams of SAT problems, separated by a 10-minute intervention. The running group also had a 10-minute cooldown afterward so their heart rates could return to normal before the second exam. Stress was measured two ways:

- **Physiological stress:** a PPG sensor on the earlobe tracked heart rate variability (HRV), and GSR sensors on two fingers tracked skin conductance.
- **Perceived stress:** a short survey adapted from the PSS-4 stress scale, taken before the first exam, after it, after the intervention, and after the second exam.

The work brought repeated failures and rounds of revision, but the team saw it through to a finished paper.

![Professor Alshurafa sits with three students, faces blurred, beneath a projected slide showing the study timeline for an exercise group and a control group across two exams](/editorial/223999890309-04.jpg "The stress team with Professor Alshurafa and their study design.")
