Running came out ahead, with the largest drop in both self-reported and physiological stress: the running group's average self-rated stress fell from 3.00 to 1.25. On the survey, meditation left self-reported stress flat at about 2, and the phone group's score dipped only slightly, from 2.25 to 2.00. Taking the sensor and survey data together, the team ranked meditation second and found that phone scrolling changed little. They concluded that running is an effective, accessible way to manage exam stress, and that meditation is a good option when running is not practical.

> "Just ten minutes of running, and I felt completely different."
> — A participating student

In September 2025, the conference returned its decision on the paper: accept.

## Three more questions, three more posters

All four papers use sensors to understand human behavior and health, and each team came at that goal from its own angle.

### TurtleTrack: a wearable for "turtle neck"

Hours hunched over phones and laptops leave many teenagers with forward head posture, the "turtle neck" that gave this project its name. The team built a neck-worn device around an inertial measurement unit (IMU) that tracks the angle of the neck in real time and detects poor posture.

In a six-person pilot, the team compared an educational video alone with the video plus real-time nudges: whenever the device's LED flagged poor posture, a supervisor clapped. Time spent in poor posture fell sharply in both groups, from 29.8% to 0.5% with the video alone and from 61.65% to 6.25% with nudging added. The students concluded that the video did much of the work and that real-time nudging helped most for the participant with the most severe posture. Their next step is a smaller, less obtrusive device that replaces the human cue with automated feedback such as a vibration motor, aimed at practical use in habit correction and wellness technology.

### Caffeine and concentration

"Does coffee really help you focus?" To find out, this team recruited 30 high school students from three schools. Each took a standardized focus test before and after a single serving of black coffee containing 180–210 mg of caffeine, while wearable sensors recorded heart rate (via PPG), skin conductance (GSR), and skin temperature.

The team saw a brief lift in concentration after caffeine, along with shifts in stress-related signals. The clearest was vascular: PPG amplitude dropped by an average of 14.2%, a sign of blood vessels constricting, and the drop was consistent across participants. On average, HRV fell 7.4% and skin conductance rose 6.8%, though heart rate and skin conductance responses varied from person to person. The team sees the data as groundwork for guidance on healthy caffeine use among teenagers.

### A breath test for gum disease

Could gum disease be detected from breath alone, without a visit to the clinic? This team paired a sensor that measures volatile sulfur compounds (VSCs), the main cause of bad breath, with machine-learning models such as Random Forest and Gradient Boosting to classify disease severity. The models were trained on de-identified records from a dental clinic in Korea, then tested on 11 participants who breathed into the sensor.

In that external test, the model reached 91% accuracy and an AUC of 1.00. The students present it as evidence that a low-cost screening tool is feasible, and they flag the small sample themselves. They plan to extend the study to larger groups, including through a collaboration with a Korean dental hospital.

## Why BSN matters

BSN is organized under the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBS) and is one of the leading international meetings for wearable sensors, healthcare AI, and biosignal analysis. It brings together researchers from institutions such as MIT, Northwestern, KAIST, UCLA, USC, Google, and DARPA, along with graduate students and medical-device companies. For these students, acceptance meant that work begun in a ten-day summer course had been reviewed and judged ready for that community.

> "Seeing data that students created presented at an international conference shows the direction research education should truly take."
> — Nabil Alshurafa, Northwestern University

The result belongs to the students. They chose the questions, designed the experiments, and kept revising until the papers were done; CRI's role was to open the path and support them along it. They were not Professor Alshurafa's only students at BSN 2025, either: a student in CRI's 1-on-1 program presented a rehabilitation wearable for runners, a story you can read on our [Student Success](/success/runners-knee-rehab-wearable-ieee-bsn) page.

Professor Alshurafa's wearable-health course is part of the [Seoul Research Program](/research/summer-camp), where small groups work directly with visiting professors, design their own studies, and write their papers in English, with CRI supporting each manuscript through submission.
